claims.text: The baseline catalyst is an equimolar nanoscale PtPdRhRuIrOs random solid solution.
Ru and Os are oxophilic elements in the PtPdRhRuIrOs catalyst.
Local atomic-scale variations in the distribution of Ru and Os modulate adsorption energies of oxygenated ethanol intermediates.
Adsorption-energy modulation caused by local elemental distributions governs ethanol-oxidation selectivity.
Adsorption-energy modulation caused by local elemental distributions governs catalyst durability.
A small decrease in oxophilic-center concentration will shift the catalyst's electronic structure.
The controlled intervention is to reduce the Ru proportion while leaving the other elements near equimolar levels.
Reducing Ru produces fewer sites that strongly bind oxygenated species.
Fewer strongly binding Ru sites adjust the adsorption energies of key ethanol-oxidation intermediates.
The adjusted adsorption energies favor pathways producing desirable products such as acetic acid.
Reducing Ru decreases catalyst degradation caused by over-oxidation.
Relative to the equimolar baseline, reduced-Ru catalysts will have improved product selectivity.
Relative to the equimolar baseline, reduced-Ru catalysts will have enhanced durability during prolonged operation.
The selectivity and durability improvements will occur without a significant loss of overall activity.
The hypothesis is restricted to acidic ethanol-oxidation conditions near ambient temperature where the catalyst remains a solid solution.
The hypothesis is restricted to compositional changes small enough to avoid phase segregation.
A systematic reduced-Ru series can be compared with the equimolar catalyst under identical ethanol-oxidation conditions.
Failure to obtain statistically significant improvements in selectivity and durability relative to the equimolar baseline would falsify the hypothesis.
Failure to observe a change in electronic structure and intermediate adsorption would falsify the proposed mechanism.
